Profile

~/profile.txt

I chose computer science to understand how the infrastructure behind everything digital actually works. My goal is clear: network administration and cybersecurity.

I want to understand systems, networks and their weaknesses so I can secure them, not just write code.

Why the DACS track

DACS stands for Deployment of Secure Communicating Applications. The track focuses on the three skills I need:

C3 Administer
configure networks, maintain secure infrastructure, understand protocols.
C1 Build
understand how an application is built, to defend it better or test it in legitimate pentesting.
C6 Collaborate
security is teamwork, with strict procedures and careful communication.

Encrypted electronic voting

~/projects/vote

10.0.20.11 VLAN 20, Year 2, in progress

A Java client-server application for running a referendum where the server counts the votes without ever being able to read a ballot.

Context
SAÉ S3.B.01 (university project)
My role
Every part: server, encryption, client, tests
Tools
Java, sockets, ElGamal

What I did

  • The server and the exchange protocol between clients and server.
  • ElGamal encryption: key generation, ballot encryption, tallying.
  • The voter’s client interface.
  • Testing, documentation and splitting the work within the group.

The network of a coworking space

~/projects/coworking

10.0.10.11 VLAN 10, Year 1, completed

Design and justify the full infrastructure of a 20-seat coworking space: hardware, addressing plan, services and open source software choices.

Context
SAÉ 2.03
My role
Architecture, addressing, choice of services
Tools
Ubuntu, VMs, Apache, MariaDB, Postfix

What I did

  • A network split into two zones, clients and servers, joined by a core switch. Internet access through a TP-Link ER605 router handling DHCP, NAT and firewalling.
  • The 192.168.1.0/24 addressing plan: static addresses for servers and workstations, DHCP for visitors on Wi-Fi.
  • Four virtualised servers on Ubuntu: web, database, mail, backup.
  • Three options compared for each service: MariaDB 11 chosen over MySQL 8.0 and PostgreSQL 16, Apache 2.4 over Nginx and Caddy, Postfix and Dovecot over Zimbra.

Cyber-Attack, an orienteering game

~/projects/cyberattaque

10.0.10.12 VLAN 10, Year 1, completed

A night-time orienteering game on campus: a rogue AI, R-AI-D, has taken over, and teams must find ten terminals to shut it down.

Context
SAÉ 2.05, project management
My role
Specifications, schedule, budget
Tools
NFC, Raspberry Pi 4, PERT, Gantt

What I did

  • NFC badges act as team IDs and health counters, scanned by volunteers dressed as zombies.
  • Standalone reboot terminals on Raspberry Pi 4 with a touchscreen, where players type simplified Bash or Python commands.
  • An app, Cyber-Map, to follow the state of the terminals and the danger zones in real time.
  • The PERT and Gantt schedule: 13 tasks, a 117-day critical path, and a justified budget.

A relational database

~/projects/bdd

10.0.10.13 VLAN 10, Year 1, completed

Design, create and populate a complete database from raw CSV files that were redundant and sometimes inconsistent.

Context
SAÉ 2.04
My role
Analysis, modelling, creation, import
Tools
Oracle, SQL, DBeaver

What I did

  • Analysing the CSVs: redundancy, functional dependencies, inconsistencies.
  • The entity-relationship model, then normalisation up to third normal form.
  • Oracle tables with their constraints: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, CHECK.
  • Importing with DBeaver after cleaning the CSVs, checked by comparing row counts.

Dominion Seaside in Java

~/projects/dominion

10.0.10.14 VLAN 10, Year 1, completed

Programming the cards of the Seaside expansion of the Dominion card game in Java.

Context
SAÉ 2.01 and 2.02
My role
Cards, duration effects, robustness
Tools
Java, OOP, MVC, Git

What I did

  • An MVC architecture separating game logic, display and player actions.
  • An abstract Card class extended by each card family: action, treasure, victory, duration.
  • Duration effects, such as Fishing Village or Lighthouse, stored and resolved at the start of the next turn, following the Observer pattern.
  • Input validation and protection against impossible states: empty hand, exhausted deck, invalid sequence.
